standard.title: Features and personal preferences
standard.description: identify features of literary texts, such as characters and settings, and give reasons for personal preferences
standard.strand: Engaging with and responding to literature
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss literary texts and share responses connecting to their own experiences (AC9E1LE02). They have not yet identified specific literary features as the basis for preference — their responses remain experience-anchored rather than feature-anchored.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify features of literary texts such as characters and settings and give reasoned explanations for personal preferences.

nodes.label: Naming features as a basis for preference
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify a specific literary feature — character, setting, plot event — as the basis for a preference, rather than giving an undifferentiated response.
nodes.minimum_width: Name one literary feature they responded to and explain why it created their preference.
nodes.typical_width: Identify multiple literary features across several texts and give reasons for preferences that reference specific features — character type, setting, narrative structure — rather than general feeling.
wider: Compare preferences for stories set in familiar vs unfamiliar worlds and discuss what makes each type appealing
Discuss preferences for characters whose lives are like or unlike their own, naming what draws them to each type

response_modes.reason: Students commonly give vague preference statements ('it was fun') or purely experiential ones ('it was like my life'). Moving to feature-anchored preference language ('I preferred the character because the setting made her actions surprising') requires exposure to multiple texts where different features create different preference responses. More texts, not more practice with one, is the productive move.

success_criteria: Student names a specific literary feature as the basis for a preference.
Student's reason references what the feature does or is, not just how they felt.

nodes.label: Responding to character behaviour
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss their feelings about characters' positive and negative behaviours and explain how these behaviours influence their preference for the text.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a character behaviour (positive or negative) and explain how it influenced their response to the text.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss responses to multiple character types — non-human characters including animals, characters with mixed behaviours — giving reasoned explanations for how behaviour shapes preference.
wider: Compare responses to the same character whose behaviour changes across a narrative — e.g. a villain who shows sympathy — and discuss how this complexity affects preference
Discuss non-human characters (animals, fantasy creatures) whose behaviour follows or subverts human expectations, and how this creates a preference response
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Complex character behaviour — mixed, contradictory, surprising — is a genuinely rich direction here. Students who can respond thoughtfully to morally complex or non-human characters are engaging with literary complexity at a level that has real depth within the Year 2 band.
success_criteria: Student can identify a character behaviour and explain how it shaped their preference for the text.
Student can distinguish between liking a character and liking a text — explaining that a preference can be based on a character they found compelling rather than likeable.
